messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Raj was a 53-year-old painter, known for his vibrant depictions of life and nature. His studio, a small, sunlit space filled with canvases, was once a sanctuary of creativity, but now it felt more like a prison of memories he couldn't escape. The traumatic event that had shattered his peace occurred three years ago, when he found himself in the midst of a civil conflict while visiting family in his native country. The explosions had been deafening, and the scent of smoke and burning debris clung to the air like a sinister reminder of the chaos. Even now, the whiff of certain paints or oils would trigger those memories, sending him spiraling into a state of hypervigilance. Each smell seemed to awaken the part of him that felt constantly on edge, convinced that danger lurked just around the corner.

As Raj navigated his daily life, he found himself haunted by auditory triggers; the sudden bang of a door or a car backfiring would cause him to jump, his body tense and ready to react as if he were still in that war zone. This startle response heightened his sense of threat, making him feel as if he had to remain watchful at all times. In the quiet moments, when he was alone with his thoughts, memories of the chaos would flood back. He often found himself reenacting the physical sensations of that day, feeling his heart race and his palms sweat as if he were reliving the trauma. Each recollection brought with it an overwhelming grief, leaving him questioning the very fabric of his existence. The story of what had happened felt so extreme that he sometimes doubted it had truly occurred, leading to a pervasive sense that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore.

Raj's negative appraisals of his situation compounded the distress. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him as an artist. The world seemed dangerous and untrustworthy, and this pervasive belief influenced his behavior. To cope, he threw himself into work, keeping busy with projects that distracted him from the haunting memories. He avoided news reports about similar conflicts, fearing they would only deepen his sense of loss and helplessness. Yet, this busyness served as a double-edged sword; while it temporarily shielded him from confronting his trauma, it also meant that the grief and memories never truly dissipated. Instead, they lay dormant, ready to resurface at the slightest provocation.

The relationship between Raj's negative appraisals and his maladaptive strategies was evident in how he managed his days. Each time he felt overwhelmed by memories of his trauma, he would push himself harder to work, believing that if he could just keep busy, he could stave off the pain. However, this only reinforced his sense of inadequacy and failure; the more he ruminated on why the event had happened to him, the more he felt trapped in a cycle of despair and avoidance. The act of painting, once a joyful expression of his identity, became a battleground where he fought against his own thoughts, yet the colors never seemed to satisfy the grief that weighed heavily on his heart.

Over time, Raj's world narrowed as his avoidance behaviors took hold. He stopped attending social gatherings, convinced that people would not understand his pain, and he withdrew from conversations that might touch on his experiences. The isolation deepened his sense of danger; he felt the world was a threatening place, one that could erupt into chaos at any moment. Each day, he faced the conflicting emotions of wanting connection and fearing exposure, leading to a spiraling anxiety that felt inescapable.

It was this culmination of grief, anxiety, and a sense of lost identity that finally brought Raj to seek help. Sitting in the therapist's office, he felt a mix of trepidation and hope. He was scared that the memories would overwhelm him, yet he longed for a way to reclaim the meaning he had lost and to paint again without the shadows of his past looming over him. As he shared his story, Raj pondered whether it was possible to find a path back to the vibrant life he once knew — a life where he could once again embrace the world without fear.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to the memory of the traumatic event.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals lead to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where threat leads to maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even now, the whiff of certain paints or oils would trigger those memories, sending him spiraling into a state of hypervigilance. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time the scent wafted through his studio, it not only brought back the vivid memories of chaos but also deepened his sense that he was in constant danger, as if the past was poised to repeat itself at any moment. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This startle response heightened his sense of threat, making him feel as if he had to remain watchful at all times. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When a loud noise startled him, it reinforced his belief that he was living in a world where threats could emerge from anywhere, leading him to feel even more vulnerable and exposed. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him as an artist. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every time he found himself in a crowded place, the suffocating fear reminded him of his perceived inadequacies, whispering to him that he would never be able to navigate life without succumbing to panic. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In the quiet moments, when he was alone with his thoughts, memories of the chaos would flood back. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After each vivid recollection surfaced, he caught himself thinking that he was somehow to blame for what had happened, convinced that if he had been more vigilant, he could have prevented the trauma from occurring. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
To cope, he threw himself into work, keeping busy with projects that distracted him from the haunting memories. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When the sense of threat loomed large, he found that immersing himself in art was the only way to feel somewhat secure, as it created an illusion of control in a world that felt chaotic and unpredictable. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, Raj's world narrowed as his avoidance behaviors took hold. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His deep-seated belief that the world was unsafe led him to shrink his social circle and limit his interactions, convinced that any engagement could expose him to further pain. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
It was this culmination of grief, anxiety, and a sense of lost identity that finally brought Raj to seek help. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Yet, what frightened him most was the thought that if he continued to avoid addressing these feelings, he would remain trapped in this cycle of despair, forever haunted by a past that felt inescapable. 
<<<END>>>
